## Abstract

This session introduces working with data in ecological economics: how to construct
**stylized facts** and why observation is always **theory-laden**. In the accompanying group
work, you find data and present preliminary results on the situation of your selected
country or region.

## 📊 Data sources for the figures

Every data figure in the lecture is built from **openly available data**, and the table below
says exactly where each one comes from. Use it to check a claim from the lecture — and, more
importantly, to pull the same indicators for **your own country analysis**.

On an Our World in Data chart page, the **Download** tab gives you the underlying data as a
CSV for *all* countries and years, not just the ones shown. That is usually the fastest route
to a comparable number for your country.

| Figure in the lecture | Where the data come from |
|---|---|
| Income grows, but in a very unequal fashion | [Maddison Project Database](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database) (via Our World in Data) |
| Income poverty remains a global problem | [World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform (PIP)](https://pip.worldbank.org/) |
| There has been progress with respect to income poverty | [Moatsos, "cost of basic needs" poverty](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/share-of-population-living-in-extreme-poverty-cost-of-basic-needs) (via Our World in Data) · World Bank PIP, as above |
| Reducing income poverty due to growth of GDP?! | The same two sources as the previous two rows, joined |
| GDP correlates with many development indicators | [Years of schooling](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/average-years-of-schooling-vs-gdp-per-capita) · [Child mortality](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/child-mortality-gdp-per-capita) · [Adult literacy](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/literacy-rate-vs-gdp-per-capita) · [Medical doctors](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/medical-doctors-per-1000-people-vs-gdp-per-capita) |
| The extraction of raw materials keeps increasing | [UN IRP Global Material Flows Database](https://www.materialflows.net/) ([background](https://www.resourcepanel.org/global-material-flows-database)). A scriptable but narrower alternative is the [UN SDG Indicators Database](https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/dataportal), series `EN_MAT_DOMCMPT` |
| GDP correlates with energy use and with emissions | [Energy use per capita](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/energy-use-per-capita-vs-gdp-per-capita) · [CO~2~ emissions](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/co2-emissions-vs-gdp) |
| Some countries achieved decoupling of GDP from emissions | [Consumption-based CO~2~ and GDP per capita](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/co2-emissions-and-gdp-per-capita) |
| Composite indicators also correlate with GDP | [Human Development Index](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/human-development-index-vs-gdp-per-capita) · [Augmented HDI (Prados de la Escosura)](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/human-development-index-escosura) · Maddison Project Database, as above |
| No country manages both at once | [Fanning, O'Neill, Hickel & Roux (2022), national trends data](https://goodlife.leeds.ac.uk/download-data/) |

::: {.callout-note}
## Want to rebuild the figures yourself?

Every figure above is built by two R scripts, from the data linked in the
table. They live in the
[`analysis/` folder of the course repository](https://github.com/graebnerc/EcolEcon26/tree/main/analysis),
together with a README explaining how to run them. You are welcome to change a
colour, a year range or a country selection — or to lift the approach for your
own poster.
:::

### 🍩 The country doughnuts

The two doughnut diagrams in the lecture come from the University of Leeds project
[A Good Life For All Within Planetary Boundaries](https://goodlife.leeds.ac.uk/). Its
**National Snapshots** and **Country Trends** pages will draw the same diagram for *your*
country, and the underlying figures can be downloaded from the same
[download page](https://goodlife.leeds.ac.uk/download-data/) as the scatter plot above.

### 🧭 The Atlas of Economic Complexity

The [Atlas of Economic Complexity](https://atlas.hks.harvard.edu/) (Harvard Growth Lab) is not
behind any figure in this lecture, but it is the obvious next stop for a country analysis. It
holds **50+ years of trade flows for 228 countries**: what a country exports and imports, to
and from whom, how that basket has shifted over time, and where it sits in the complexity
rankings.

- [Country profiles](https://atlas.hks.harvard.edu/countries) — start here for your country
- [Rankings](https://atlas.hks.harvard.edu/rankings) — economic complexity, and growth projections
- [Data downloads](https://atlas.hks.harvard.edu/data-downloads) — the underlying data, if you
  want to compute something yourself

A caveat worth carrying into the poster: economic complexity says something about the
**productive structure** of an economy, not about whether that structure is ecologically
sustainable or socially just. A high-complexity export basket and a transgressed material
footprint are entirely compatible — which is itself a result worth pointing at.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Two habits worth acquiring now

**Write down every judgement call.** Which year, which indicator, which source, which of
several competing series. That list is where the theory-ladenness of your own analysis
becomes visible — and it belongs on your poster.

**Check what a number actually measures** before you compare it. Poverty lines change
(the World Bank moved from 2011 to 2021 purchasing power parities, so the lines are now
$3.00 and $4.20 rather than $1.90 and $3.20), and material *extraction* is not material
*consumption*. Two defensible sources can tell two different stories about the same country.
:::

### 🏆 Further readings

*On how a measurement choice makes the result:*

- @reddy2010 — the classic critique of the dollar-a-day poverty line.
- @jerven2013 — how development statistics are actually produced, and what that
  means for anyone using them.

*On the doughnut, and on its critics:*

- @fanning2022 — the study behind the scatter plot in the lecture.
- @fanning2025 — the 2025 successor, with 35 indicators up to 2022, at the
  global level.
- @grabner-radkowitsch2026 — an introduction to doughnut economics (in German).
- @winter2026 — a critical reading of the doughnut *diagram* itself.

*On objectivity:*

- @harding2015 — the source of the two passages on strong objectivity quoted in
  the lecture.
